parts.title: Enrolling for an evening class
parts.context: A woman phones a college to enrol on an evening class.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman telephoning a college to enrol on an evening class. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Good evening, Brackenfield College, evening class enrolment. Gareth speaking.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Oh, hello. I'm phoning about your evening classes. I'd like to sign up for one of the photography courses, if there are still places.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Ah, digital photography. That's one of our most popular courses. I'll take a few details from you, and then we'll see what we can do.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The woman wants to join a photography course, so 'photography' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Right, could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Yes, it's Rosa Whitcombe.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Sorry, could you spell your surname for me?

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Of course. It's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Thanks. And your address?

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: It's seventy-two Hartley Road. Oh, sorry, no, I always say that the wrong way round. Twenty-seven, not seventy-two.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: No problem. And how did you hear about the course?

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Well, I picked up your brochure in the library, but the real reason is that my sister did the pottery course here last year. She enjoyed it so much that she talked me into trying something myself.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Good for her. Now, the course runs on two evenings, Tuesday and Thursday. Which would you prefer?

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Thursday, please, if possible. I play badminton on Tuesdays.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: I'm afraid the Thursday class has been full since August. There are still a few places on the Tuesday one, though.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Oh, that's a shame. Well, I suppose I can move my badminton to another night. I'll take Tuesday, then.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Lovely. Both classes run from seven until nine, for ten weeks.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: And how much does it cost? The brochure says one hundred and twenty pounds.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Ah, that's last year's price, I'm afraid. It's gone down this year, to 95 pounds for the whole course, thanks to a grant from the council.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Now, the college term starts on the fourteenth of January, but the first photography class isn't until the following week, on the twenty-first.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Is it in the main building? I've never been to the college before.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: No, it's in the new Hawthorn Building, on the third floor, in room 36. There's a lift, if you don't fancy the stairs.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Great. Do I need to bring anything with me?

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: You'll need your own camera, of course, but it doesn't have to be an expensive one. And you should bring a tripod as well. The college only has a few to lend, and they go very quickly.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: OK. And is there an exam at the end?

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: No exam. Instead, in the last week there's a public exhibition of everyone's work, held in the town gallery. A lot of people bring their families along.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: That sounds lovely. One last thing: is there anywhere to park? I'll be coming straight from work.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: There's a car park behind the Hawthorn Building. It's two pounds an hour until six o'clock, but after that it's free, and as your class doesn't start until seven, you'll be fine.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Perfect. Thank you very much.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: You're welcome, Ms Whitcombe. I'll email you a confirmation this evening, and we'll see you in January.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A visit to a railway museum
parts.context: A guide gives a talk to visitors at a small railway museum.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide giving a talk to a group of visitors at a small railway museum. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Aldercombe Railway Museum. My name's Margaret, and I'll be your guide today. First, a little background.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: Many people assume that a branch line like ours was built for holidaymakers, and it did carry plenty of them in later years. But when it opened in 1871, the purpose was much more practical. The quarries in the hills needed a way of getting their slate down to the harbour at Port Elwick, and the railway did exactly that.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: It closed in 1966. Visitors often tell me that was because the viaduct had become unsafe, but it had been repaired years earlier, and the quarries were still busy. The real problem was that most families now had a car, or took the bus, and the trains were running almost empty.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: After the closure, the station stood empty, and the council planned to demolish it. But local people, including several retired railway workers, formed a society to save it, and the museum opened in 1988. Now, we've bought a few things at auction, and a national museum has lent us some signalling equipment, but most of what you'll see was donated by families in the valley, who'd kept things in their attics for years.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: We're a charity, run almost entirely by volunteers. We actually have more people offering to help than we can use, and visitor numbers are the highest for ten years. Our big worry is the roof of the engine shed, which leaks badly. Replacing it will cost nearly eighty thousand pounds, which is a great deal for a small museum.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: Our star exhibit is Number Seven, a steam locomotive from 1923, which you'll find in the engine shed. She doesn't run any more, so I'm afraid there are no rides. Some visitors ask to watch our engineers at work, but that area is closed for safety reasons. What you can do is climb up into the driver's cab, which children especially love.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: Now, let me explain the layout. Please look at the map. We're standing just inside the main entrance, at the bottom. Straight ahead is the station building, with the ticket office and the museum shop. The toilets are on the left, next to the car park, in case anyone needs them before we set off.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: Let's start at the west end. If you go through the station building onto the platform and turn left, you can walk right to the end, and just beyond it you'll find the signal box. You're welcome to go inside and pull the levers.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: Back at the front of the station building, turn right, and the first building you come to is the café. It's in the old goods shed, and it closes at three.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: Now, if you go back down towards the entrance, you'll see the model railway, in the old warehouse. Directly across the path from the car park. The children love it.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: To see our restoration work, return to the platform and use the foot crossing to cross the line. Just beyond the crossing, on the right, is the carriage workshop, where volunteers are restoring old carriages.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: And on the other side of the crossing, to the left, there's a large field, which is our picnic area, with tables in the shade. Further along on the right, beyond the workshop, there's a small play area, but that's only for younger children.

script.speaker: margaret
script.text: Right, if there are no questions, shall we make a start? Please follow me.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A project on sleep and memory
parts.context: Two psychology students discuss their project with a tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students, Hannah and Jamal, discussing a project on sleep and memory with their tutor, Dr Reid. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: Come in, both of you. Before we discuss the pilot, remind me why you chose sleep and memory. I think it was on my list of suggestions.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: It was, but that's not why we picked it. We went to the talk by the visiting researcher in October, and we both found it fascinating.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: I'm a terrible sleeper myself, but that's not why. It was the talk that made me want to study it properly.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: Fair enough. So, how did the pilot go?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Mostly fine. One person forgot to come back for the second session, but that's normal. The real problem was the test itself. The word pairs were far too easy, so nearly everyone scored thirty-eight or more out of forty.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: So there's no room to see any difference. What will you change?

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: Well, Hannah wanted longer lists, but then the session would last over an hour. Her other idea was pictures instead of words, but they're much harder to score. So we're keeping forty pairs, but making them completely unrelated, like a candle and a tractor.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: Good. That's the standard solution. And who does what in the main study?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: I offered to run all the sessions, with Jamal doing the statistics.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: But if only one of us meets the participants, the instructions might not always be the same. So we'll both be at every session, and Hannah will do the analysis, because she's better at it than I am.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: There's something else, Dr Reid. We wondered about a third group, who would stay awake all night.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: I'd advise against it. The ethics committee might object, but that's not my main worry. If that group remembers less, you wouldn't know whether it was because they hadn't slept, or just because they were too tired to concentrate. The results would be impossible to interpret.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: I see. We'll stick to two groups, then.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: Right, now the plan for the main study. I'll tell you what I think of each part. First, participants. How many are you hoping to recruit?

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: Twenty-four, so twelve in each group.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: Hmm. That's rather few for comparing two groups. If the effect is small, you won't be able to show it. Try to get at least forty.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: OK. At the moment, one group is tested at nine in the morning, and the other at nine in the evening.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: That worries me. People are simply sharper at some times of day than others, so you'd never know whether a difference came from sleep or from the clock. Both groups need to be tested at the same time of day.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: And how will you measure the sleep itself?

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: A diary that people fill in each morning.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: Hmm. A student who's been up until three won't necessarily admit it. The department has wristbands that record movement during the night, so you'd have hard figures that don't depend on what people tell you.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: And what does the information sheet say about the study?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: That we're investigating whether sleep helps memory.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: I'd leave that out. If participants know what you expect, the sleep group may try harder without realising it. Just say it's a study of memory, and explain the full aim afterwards.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: Finally, the report. Nearly all your participants will be students, aged eighteen to twenty-two, and young people sleep very differently from older adults. In the discussion, point out that your findings may not apply to everyone.

script.speaker: reid
script.text: Oh, and you needn't go back to the ethics committee. You're only changing the timetable, so your existing approval is fine.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: That's a relief. Thank you, Dr Reid.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how medieval maps were made
parts.context: A lecture about how maps were made in medieval Europe.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how maps were made in medieval Europe. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I want to look at medieval maps, and in particular at how they were actually made, because every single one of them was a hand-made object. There was no printing of maps in Europe until the late fifteenth century, so each map had to be drawn one at a time, and very often copied from another.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Let's start with the materials. You might expect paper, but paper was still rare and expensive for much of the period. The papyrus used by the Romans was no use either, because it rots in the damp European climate. So what they normally used was parchment, which is animal skin that has been scraped and stretched until it is thin and smooth. It might come from sheep, goats or calves.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The pen was a quill, which is simply a large feather, usually from a goose, cut to a point with a small knife. Colours came from natural materials, ground up and mixed with egg, and gold leaf was sometimes added for the most important buildings.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Next, where did mapmakers get their information? Well, perhaps surprisingly, they hardly ever went anywhere themselves. A mapmaker was usually a scholar working at a desk, using written descriptions by ancient authors, and the stories of travellers. Soldiers and merchants contributed a few details, but the most valuable accounts came from pilgrims, who often wrote guides to the routes they had followed. Nobody surveyed the land, of course, so distances were usually estimated in days of travel.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The best-known kind of medieval map is the mappa mundi, or world map. These were not meant for finding your way. They were designed to show how the world fitted into the Christian story, and many were displayed in cathedrals. The layout reflects that purpose. Jerusalem was usually placed at the centre, as the holiest city. And the map was turned so that east was at the top, rather than north, which is where we get the word orientation. Around the edges, where mapmakers had no real information, they drew monsters, such as men with dogs' heads, and huge sea serpents.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Sea charts, known as portolan charts, were quite different, because they were practical tools. From about 1300, ships in the Mediterranean used charts that were drawn from the observations of other sailors: the courses they had steered by compass, and the distances they thought they had covered. The magnetic compass, which had reached Europe in the twelfth century, made all this possible, and the results are surprisingly accurate. Straight lines radiate across the chart from compass roses, helping the captain to choose a direction. The names of ports are written at right angles to the coast, mostly in black ink, but the most important ports are always written in red. Almost nothing is shown inland, since that was of no interest to a sailor.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, the question of copying. Because making a map was so time-consuming, maps were usually copied rather than made from scratch. For much of the Middle Ages, the copyists were monks, working in the writing rooms of monasteries. Every copyist made small mistakes, and those mistakes were copied again, so an error could survive for centuries. This began to change around the year 1400, when scholars in Italy rediscovered the work of Ptolemy, a Greek geographer from ancient Alexandria. He had listed places by their coordinates, using lines of latitude and longitude, and that idea gradually changed the way maps were drawn.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So a medieval map is really a mixture: part guidebook, part history lesson, part religious teaching and, in the case of sea charts, part practical instrument. That's all for today. Next week, we'll look at how printing changed the map trade.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
